note: Fourteen printables, plus 01b — an A3 alternative to the sound-frame mat, made by the same builder and by the Writing Shelf generator at /montree/library/tools/writing-shelf-generator. All adult-facing text sits outside the cards. CUT ONCE: cards butt against each other with no gutters, and every cut line runs the full width or the full height of the page, edge to edge, so one straight stroke of the blade separates the cards on both sides of it. The lines are light-grey 0.25 mm hairlines — they are cut away, so a line IS the card edge — and a small black triangle at the 5.5 mm printer-safe margin marks each line where it meets the paper edge, because a hairline dies in the last few millimetres of any printer. Card content stops 4 mm inside every card edge, so a wandering blade never touches a photograph or a word. Footer on every sheet: “Cut along every grey line · N cards”. Sheets 02, 03, 06, 13 and 14 are MOUNTED on coloured backing card with a 1 cm border, so their printed size is 20 mm smaller than the finished card; 04, 05, 09, 11 and 12 are not mounted and print at finished size. Sheet 14’s backing card is not any colour: PINK for its tier 1 cards, BLUE for its tier 2 and GREEN for its tier 3, because on that sheet the colour IS the reading level. Sheet 12’s word card is the same 60 × 35 mm as sheet 04’s heart word, set in the same face at the same size on the same baseline, so a heart word off the Tray 4 ring and a word out of the Tray 5 tin sit as one sentence on the sentence line.

items.title: Story starter cards ×14 — 80 × 120 mm
items.note: The supplement that unsticks Tray 5. A child who can read every card in the tin can still sit in front of an empty sentence line, because inventing a sentence out of nothing is a bigger leap than reading one. He pulls a card, says what he sees, builds THAT out of the tin — and then turns the card over. The back carries the one decodable sentence the picture is of, so the card corrects him itself and no adult has to be standing there. Not tied to any one lesson: it is on the tray all year. Same card as sheets 02 and 03 — 80 × 120 mm printed, mounted on coloured backing card to 100 × 140 — because these are picked up and physically TURNED, which is what a flip card is for. THE SENTENCE IS LOWER CASE and set in Comic Neue — teacher review of the printed proofs, 2026-09-12. These are the literal words a four-year-old says when he looks at the picture (“hen in a pen”, not “Hen in a pen”); the capital and the full stop are his to add with a punctuation tile off the tray. Comic Neue is the free SIL-OFL face metrically similar to Comic Sans MS, which is Microsoft-licensed and cannot be embedded in a PDF the shelf ships; adult text in the margin is still Andika. THE CARD FRAME IS NEW, and it is the whole of the second round of proofs (2026-09-12): the 1.5 mm square-cornered rule printed as a thin line floating in a large white margin — “a line someone drew” — rather than as a designed card. It is now a ROUNDED DOUBLE FRAME, identical on sheets 13 and 14 and imported constant for constant so the two decks cannot drift: 2.6 mm of stroke with a 5 mm outer corner radius, its OUTER edge 4 mm off the cut line on all four sides so the bleed the blade works into is even the whole way round, and a 0.4 mm hairline of the same colour 2.2 mm inside it, cornered to match. The double rule is the playing-card and certificate cue. Content sits 0.8 mm inside the hairline, square on all four sides, in a 60 × 100 mm box. EVERY ONE OF THE FOURTEEN IS FRAMED, on both faces, AND THE FRAME COLOUR IS THE READING TIER — sheet 14’s Montessori pink / blue / green, the three hexes imported from that sheet’s builder so they cannot drift. The deck used to be framed in a neutral warm charcoal with “hen in a pen” alone in pink, and a neutral says nothing: a child cannot sort the tray by it and a teacher cannot hand out a level with it. Each card is now read against the classroom’s own three-colour code on the words printed on its back. PINK (#D45B86) is every content word a pure three-letter CVC, one sound a letter, and it takes TEN of the fourteen: cat on a mat, pig in a wig, hen in a pen, dog on a log, fox in a box, bug on a rug, rat in a hat, nut in a hut, ant on a pan, cub in a tub — “ant” is filed with the three-letter short-vowel words, and so are “fox” and “box”, the x notwithstanding. BLUE (#2F5FA6) is four letters or more with no consonant blend, and it takes NONE: every card on this deck that leaves three-letter CVC behind leaves it for a blend. The tier is wired through the builder all the same, so a future blue card frames, paginates and labels itself with no other change. GREEN (#2F7D4F) is a consonant blend anywhere on the card, and it takes FOUR: frog in a bog (fr), bee on a tree (tr), duck in a truck (tr), sheep asleep (sl, over the sh digraph). ONE TIER TO A PRINTED PAGE. The deck is ordered pink then green and a page is filled from one tier only, then left short rather than topped up from the next — the teacher prints each tier onto matching coloured card stock, so a mixed page is a page he cannot use. Ten pink cards at four a page is three pink sheets of 4 + 4 + 2, the two blank slots on the third being correct and not a gap to plug; the four green cards fill the fourth sheet. Every page header names its tier on both the picture side and the sentence side. THE GROUND IS PAPER WHITE ON EVERY CARD (2026-09-13). “bee on a tree” is drawn on a scanned textured sheet whose grain runs 226–245 within one picture. This sheet used to white-point a ground by the MEDIAN of its border, which puts the middle of that grain at paper white and leaves the dark half of it below — so the card printed as a soft grey box with a visible edge, the one thing a picture card must not have. It now uses the same paper() as sheet 14, imported rather than copied: the white point is taken BELOW the grain, at the 5th percentile of the border band and floored so art touching the border cannot drag it down, and everything above it clips to paper. Two of the fourteen are white-pointed (pig-wig, bee-tree); the other twelve were already paper and are left completely alone. THE ART IS TRIMMED TO ITS OWN INK AND FILLS THE BOX. The source drawings carry whatever white margin the generator gave them, and on the proofs that margin printed as dead space round a small subject. The builder now measures each drawing’s ink at build time — the box holding all but 0.2 % of its ink WEIGHT at each edge, so soft pencil shading and a light wash are kept while the fading tip of a ground scribble is not — crops to it, gives back an even 2 % breathing margin and fits the result into the whole 60 × 100 mm content box, aspect preserved and centred ON THE INK, which is also what fixed drawings printing low in the card. Every card reaches the full 60 mm width; a wide composition is simply shorter. The source files are never written to. ONE EM FOR BOTH DECKS. The sentence size is no longer a per-card result: 10.90 mm of em, a 7.3 mm cap height — three times the cap height of a reading book — sets every sentence on sheets 13 and 14, and a sentence of three words or fewer sets on ONE line wherever it fits at that em. The old wrap took whatever size each sentence could reach, so “the cat sat” and “the ant sat” set large on one line while “the sun sat” — the same eleven characters — broke to two and came out visibly smaller. A longer sentence takes the fewest lines that fit at that same em, so the deck steps down in line count and never in type size. Holding EVERY three-word sentence to one line without exception would peg the em to the longest of them, “the penguin spat”, at 8.4 mm — a small line of type adrift in a large white card, too timid to be read at arm’s length by the child it is for, and a waste of the frame. Letting that one card wrap to “the penguin / spat” costs one card on one green sheet and buys 30 % bigger letterforms on every other card in both decks. Six of sheet 13’s fourteen and seven of sheet 14’s eighteen take two or three lines at this em; the rest set on one, and every one of them sets at the same size.

items.title: Illustrated sentence cards ×18 — pink, blue and green, 80 × 120 mm
items.note: The graded picture-then-words card for Tray 5. Sheet 12 gives the tray its tin of loose words; this sheet gives it eighteen pictures, each with its one sentence on the BACK. He meets the picture, says what he sees, builds that out of the tin — and then TURNS THE CARD OVER and reads the line, which corrects him without an adult standing there. The sentence used to sit under the picture on the same face; teacher review of the printed proofs (2026-09-12) sent that back, because a picture with its words beside it is a LABEL and the child reads the words and stops looking. FRONT = the picture and nothing else, BACK = the sentence and nothing else: the Montessori three-part card, and sheet 13's structure exactly. THREE TIERS, AND THE COLOUR IS THE DIFFICULTY OF THE WORDS — the Montessori Pink, Blue and Green reading series: pink is pure three-letter CVC (the cat sat, a pig in a wig), blue is four letters or more with no blend (the ant naps, the cat digs), green is consonant blends, one blend a card (st, sp, bl, cr, nd, mp). ONE CARD IS CARRIED, and it keeps its own colour (2026-09-13): “a fox in a box” is pink WORK — fox and box are three-letter words, and sheet 13 prints that same pair pink — but it sits at the HEAD OF THE BLUE GROUP because the teacher wanted one already-known card at the start of the harder tray, for familiarity. It keeps its POSITION in blue and its PINK FRAME. A pink card at the head of the blue tray says “you already know this one”; painting it blue would claim a difficulty the words do not have and would put the same two words in two different colours across the two Tray 5 decks. The carry is recorded in the data — card(..., carriedFrom: 1) in writing-shelf-language.ts, which sets frameTier and a carried flag — so it is not “corrected” back. Since 2026-09-13 the deck is imposed ONE GROUP TO A SHEET, so the carried card lands on the FIRST BLUE SHEET (sheet 3) as the single pink-framed card among three blue-framed ones — the clearest form of the signal, and that sheet still prints onto blue card stock. Its header reads “blue”, which names the group on it. The card carries NO written difficulty label, exactly as a pink-series card has never had “pink series” printed on it: ONE EVEN COLOUR FRAME round the content, the same on both faces and the same width on all four sides, is the whole signal. The solid colour bar that used to run along the top of the card is gone — it was the top of the border, and on the proof it read, correctly, as a border thicker on one side than the others. Mount tier 1 on PINK card, tier 2 on BLUE and tier 3 on GREEN and the tray sorts itself. THE CARD FRAME IS NEW, and it is the whole of the second round of proofs (2026-09-12): the 1.5 mm square-cornered rule printed as a thin line floating in a large white margin — “a line someone drew” — rather than as a designed card. The double rule is the playing-card and certificate cue. Content sits 0.8 mm inside the hairline, square on all four sides, in a 60 × 100 mm box. The frame colour is still the only tier signal: no bars, no labels, no dots. Comic Neue is the free SIL-OFL face metrically similar to Comic Sans MS, which is Microsoft-licensed and cannot be embedded in a shipped PDF; adult text in the margin is still Andika. Same 80 × 120 card as sheets 02, 03 and 13, so it takes the same 100 mm stands, and the same SHORT-EDGE duplex registration. TIER 3 IS COMPLETE at six: mp — “the cat can jump” — landed with its drawing on 2026-09-12. Fifteen of the eighteen pictures are REUSED art — the Dark Phonics picture books (the-sat’s flashcard tiles, the-sad, the-hot, the-nap, the-dig, the-spat), the satpin-v2 story starters, the satpin-v2 CVC set (w08-sand), and fox-box, which is the same drawing sheet 13 already prints; only green’s blob, crab and jump were drawn for it, and they live in phonics-images/satpin-v2/blends/. Sheet 12 has since grown sun, hot and digs, so every pink and blue sentence can now be BUILT out of the tin as well as read. Tier 3’s blend words (star, penguin, blob, crab, dad, sand, jump) are outside the tin by design — a blend is past where the tin stops — so the green cards are reading-and-copying work; see SENTENCE_BUILDER_GAPS. THE ART IS TRIMMED TO ITS OWN INK AND FILLS THE BOX. items.cut: Cut along every grey line — two strokes across the sheet, two down it, edge to edge — for four butted cards of 80 × 120 mm. Mounted on a coloured backing card with a 1 cm border they finish at 100 × 140 mm. Black triangles in the margin mark every line; they land in the same place on both faces, so front cuts and back cuts coincide. ONE GROUP TO A SHEET (2026-09-13), so each sheet prints onto its own colour of card stock: eighteen cards are SIX sheets (twelve pages, duplex) — pink on sheets 1–2 (4 + 2), blue on sheets 3–4 (4 + 2), green on sheets 5–6 (4 + 2). Each group's second sheet carries TWO cards and two blank slots; those six blanks are deliberate and are never topped up from the next group. Sheet 3, the first blue sheet, carries the CARRIED, pink-framed “a fox in a box” beside three blue-framed cards — the one card on the blue stock that is not blue, which is exactly the “you already know this one” signal it is there to give. items.howToPrint: Print 6 sheets DUPLEX, flip on SHORT EDGE, 100% in colour on card; four 80 × 120 mm cards per sheet, the picture on the front and its sentence on the back.
